experiment_design.technical_details: This study designs a computational framework to test the hypothesis that Material Flow Analysis (MFA) using only publicly available data can identify economically feasible plastic waste interventions in Small Island Developing States (SIDS). The technical approach involves constructing a static MFA model for a representative SIDS (e.g., Trinidad and Tobago, as referenced in the knowledge gap context, or a proxy like Mauritius if data is more accessible) using data from UN Comtrade, World Bank Open Data, and national statistical offices. The model will map plastic inflows (imports/production), stocks (in-use), and outflows (waste generation, recycling, leakage). Economic feasibility will be assessed by coupling the MFA outputs with a simplified Cost-Benefit Analysis (CBA) module, estimating costs of collection/recycling vs. revenue from recovered materials or avoided landfill fees. Environmental benefits will be estimated using standard emission factors for avoided virgin production. The core validation is a 'data sufficiency stress test': determining if the uncertainty bounds derived from public data proxies are narrow enough to distinguish between positive and negative Net Present Value (NPV) for specific interventions.

experiment_design.technical_details: This study designs a computational framework to test the hypothesis that Material Flow Analysis (MFA) using only publicly available data can identify economically feasible plastic waste interventions in Small Island Developing States (SIDS). The technical approach involves constructing a static MFA model for a representative SIDS (e.g., Trinidad and Tobago, as referenced in the knowledge gap context, or a proxy like Mauritius if data is more accessible) using data from UN Comtrade, World Bank Open Data, and national statistical offices. The model will map plastic inflows (imports/production), stocks (in-use), and outflows (waste generation, recycling, leakage). Economic feasibility will be assessed by coupling the MFA outputs with a simplified Cost-Benefit Analysis (CBA) module, estimating costs of collection/recycling vs. revenue from recovered materials or avoided landfill fees. Environmental benefits will be estimated using standard emission factors for avoided virgin production. The core validation is a 'data sufficiency stress test': determining if the uncertainty bounds derived from public data proxies are narrow enough to distinguish between positive and negative Net Present Value (NPV) for specific interventions.

experiment_design.technical_details: This study designs a computational framework to test the hypothesis that Material Flow Analysis (MFA) using only publicly available data can identify economically feasible plastic waste interventions in Small Island Developing States (SIDS). The technical approach involves constructing a static MFA model for a representative SIDS (e.g., Trinidad and Tobago, as referenced in the knowledge gap context, or a proxy like Mauritius if data is more accessible) using data from UN Comtrade, World Bank Open Data, and national statistical offices. The model will map plastic inflows (imports/production), stocks (in-use), and outflows (waste generation, recycling, leakage). Economic feasibility will be assessed by coupling the MFA outputs with a simplified Cost-Benefit Analysis (CBA) module, estimating costs of collection/recycling vs. revenue from recovered materials or avoided landfill fees. Environmental benefits will be estimated using standard emission factors for avoided virgin production. The core validation is a 'data sufficiency stress test': determining if the uncertainty bounds derived from public data proxies are narrow enough to distinguish between positive and negative Net Present Value (NPV) for specific interventions.
